entries.title: Two people killed as bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest
entries.summary: The bus was traveling from Italy to Munich, carrying 33 Filipino tourists who wanted to visit the famous beer festival. One of the dozens injured remains in life-threatening condition.
entries.content:
Germany

Two people killed after bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest

September 27, 2026

The bus was traveling from Italy to Munich, carrying 33 Filipino tourists who wanted to visit the famous beer festival. One of the dozens injured remains in life-threatening condition.

Two people were killed and many more injured when a bus carrying a group of Filipino tourists overturned in southern Germany on Sunday en route to the Munich Oktoberfest.

The bus was coming from Milan, an Italian city with a large Filipino community.

According to German police, there were 33 tourists on the bus when, at 5:41 a.m. local time (03:41 a.m. GMT), the vehicle went off the side of the A96 highway and overturned. No other vehicles were involved in the crash.

Six of the injured were immediately rushed by helicopter to nearby hospitals, one of whom was thought to still be in a life-threatening condition. Two more were taken by ambulance to the hospital, while another 22 were first treated at the scene before several of those were also brought to the hospital.

Police so far have only identified one of the two people who died as a 58-year-old Filipino citizen.

"It is naturally very chaotic at first, and establishing the facts is difficult,” explained a spokesperson for the local police headquarters. It took police hours to confirm how many people actually were on the bus.

Bus driver charged with negligent homicide

In addition to the 33 tourists, there were the two Italian bus drivers on board, both of whom were not injured in the crash. The driver who was at the wheel at the time of the crash is now being investigated for negligent homicide, police said. "That is standard procedure,” a police spokeswoman explained.

The cause of the accident remained unclear, police said. "The public prosecutor's office has commissioned an accident reconstruction expert report to determine the cause of the crash. It is far too early to comment.”

More than 200 firefighters, medics and police were rushed to the scene of the crash. A section of the highway was completely blocked for some time before, but in the afternoon, traffic was allowed to resume.

There have been a string of bus accidents in recent weeks. Earlier in September, a Dutch coach crashed in Switzerland, killing five, while a bus crash on Germany's A3 highway left 30 people injured.

Oktoberfest draws millions of visitors

Munich’s Oktoberfest is the world’s largest beer festival, attracting millions of visitors to the Bavarian capital each year. Held over roughly two weeks, it combines giant beer tents, traditional Bavarian food, live music and fairground rides, drawing visitors from Germany and around the world.

This year, the Oktoberfest runs from September 19 to October 4. Organizers said that at the halfway point, around 3.8 million people had already visited the festival — about 300,000 more than at the same point last year.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
entries.summary: French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.
entries.content:
France

Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit

September 27, 2026

French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.

Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine, located near the Spanish border, is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."

Later, the pope also said it was "impossible to regard causing death as something normal."

"What is legal is not necessarily moral," he added, in what could be seen as a reference to France's euthanasia and assisted suicide law which came into effect last month.

"We must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," said the 71-year-old pontiff.

Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.

A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.

While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."

But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.

"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."

Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."

 "You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: UK: 5 arrested after 'major incident' near Fairford air base
entries.summary: Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had been arrested.
entries.content:
September 27, 2026

Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had been arrested.

British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning.

London's Metropolitan police said five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a "terrorist act" and explosive-related offenses.

The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines. The authorities said they believed the incident to be "contained."

Counter-terrorism police were leading the probe.

"We are in the early stages of an investigation," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said in an online statement, adding that the authorities were "working closely with our partners" to understand the circumstances of the incident.

The statement urged the public to share any information they may have related to the issue.

Bomb disposal units examining three 'suspicious vehicles'

Local police said they had received a call overnight on Sunday about "three suspicious vehicles" heading to the base.

"Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area," assistant chief constable Richard Ocone told reporters.

He added that a cordon of 400 meters, or approximately 1/4 of a mile, has been put in place around the vehicles "while the army's explosive ordinance disposal unit examine them."

"As a precaution, around 85 households have been advised to evacuate while these examinations take place," Ocone said.

He added that some of the evacuees were taken to a nearby leisure center.

The Gloucestershire police representative also asked the public "not to speculate" but follow official channels instead.

Officials stay tight-lipped

A spokesperson for ​the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take ⁠appropriate ​actions to ensure the safety and security of our ​US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families."

The background for the incident was not immediately clear.

The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer. The evacuations also come at a time of heightened tensions in Northern Ireland, and less than two months after Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone at the Leipzig airport, which its authorities attributed to Russia.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
entries.summary: In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.
entries.content:
France

European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing

September 27, 2026

In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.

In the European Union's most populous city, pressure on the housing market is so great that many of its residents are willing to undertake a historic experiment: Five years ago, Berliners voted in a referendum to instruct the Senate of the German capital to draft a law that would put an end to the power of large real estate companies. Those that owned more than 3,000 units should be expropriated, they said. The Senate did not act on the results of the referendum, which was non-binding. Meanwhile, the average cost of new leases has since risen by about half.

But in the Berlin elections on September 20, the socialist Left Party, which in its campaign had promised to act on the referendum, won the largest share of the vote. Whether it will be able to make good on its promises now depends on how negotiations to form a coalition shape up. But whatever happens, the election has drawn attention once again to the severity of the housing crisis in many cities across Europe.

Here are some initiatives that have already been put in place:

Vienna: The city is the landlord

The Vienna model is a flagship solution to soaring rent prices in Europe. The ambitious social housing program as introduced after World War I when the Austrian capital experienced a severe housing crisis. Beds were so scarce that some workers had to sleep in shifts. Diseases such as tuberculosis spread in the cramped living conditions. 

The model serves to stabilize the city's housing market to this day: According to the Vienna authorities, the city owns approximately 220,000 municipal apartments that it rents out as well as 200,000 subsidized dwellings. More than 60% of Vienna's residents live in one of these two types of housing. This also helps to stabilize prices on the private market.

Basel: Public land, private buildings

The fact that housing is becoming increasingly expensive in many cities is largely due to the fact that a city's attractiveness is reflected in land prices. In many places, people are considering how to decouple rents from the price of land. One means of doing this is not to sell municipal land but to lease it to cooperatives or socially-conscious investors. This benefits councils that do not have to bear construction costs and developers too, as they do not have to factor in exorbitant land costs that are ultimately passed on to tenants.

The Swiss city of Basel is one of the pioneers of this model. About 40% of all cooperative housing units are located on public land. The Spanish city of Barcelona and the Portuguese capital Lisbon have also stepped up efforts to put this model in place.

Paris: Buying back office buildings and converting them into homes

It is harder if land and buildings are in private hands. In 2014, the French capital Paris launched an anti-displacement plan giving the municipality a "first right of refusal" in gentrifying neighborhoods to increase the share of affordable housing in the city. The current target is 30% social housing for low-income residents by 2035

Earlier this year, the French government and the Paris regional authorities identified 61 projects that could convert empty office buildings into housing and create up to 8,200 homes in the inner suburbs of the French capital.

Prague: Apartments for public-sector workers

The Czech capital has found another way to keep those without whom the city could not function in Prague: caregivers, police officers, teachers and sanitation workers. Some 660 new energy-efficient apartments reserved specifically for public-sector employees have just been built.

The subsidiary of a Czech bank, which has received European loans, handled the development. The aim is to keep rents 20% below the market rate thanks to economies of scale, and it is not the bank who decides on the tenants but hospitals or public sector agencies, which draw up leases and can attract new employees with affordable rent options. More apartments are currently being planned.

Dublin: Non-profit cost rental housing

It has also become difficult for people with low incomes to stay in the Irish capital Dublin. During and after Ireland's financial crisis of 2008, foreign investors bought up a lot of real estate and at the same time rents skyrocketed when several major tech companies chose Dublin as their EU headquarters because of favorable tax rates. There are now long waiting lists for public housing in the city whose supply remains too low.

In 2021, the Irish government introduced the Cost Rental Housing program to provide housing to those on middle incomes, i.e. those who earn too much to qualify for public housing but too little to have a chance on the private market. To qualify in Dublin, a household has to have a net income of below €66,000 ($75,000) per year. Non-profits or public agencies lease out the apartments and rents are below market levels, by an average of almost 30% according to a recent study by the Dublin-based Economic & Social Research Institute (ESRI).

The Irish government hopes to be able to deliver 18,000 low-cost rental homes by the end of the decade. Last year, there were more than 4,200 applicants for 104 apartments in a new community in a suburb of Dublin.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality
entries.summary: Early projections show Swiss voters rejecting a stricter application of the country's vaunted neutrality. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.
entries.content:
Switzerland

Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality

September 27, 2026

Early projections show Swiss voters rejecting a stricter application of the country's vaunted neutrality. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.

Voters in Switzerland   look set to reject a proposal for stricter neutrality in a referendum held on Sunday, according to projections by state broadcaster SRF.

According to SRF figures, 29% voted for tighter rules on neutrality while 71% voted against adopting stricter measures.

Although Swiss ‌neutrality has ⁠been recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, exactly how the government implements it is not clearly specified.

The initiative was brought forward by the Pro Schweiz association, a right-wing organization with links to the right-wing populist Swiss People's Party. They argue that the Swiss government has moved too close to the European Union and NATO since Russia's war in Ukraine.

What the Pro Schweiz Association wanted to achieve

The group said its aims were for:

  • Swiss neutrality to be applied "permanently and without exception"
  • Switzerland to maintain an army capable of defense
  • Switzerland not to get involved in conflicts between third parties
  • Switzerland not to join a defense alliance unless attacked
  • The UN to approve any sanctions before Switzerland joins them

Swiss sentiment on neutrality

According to a poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) earlier this month, the move toward a stricter interpretation of Swiss neutrality does not have the traction needed to pass a referendum. Some 63% of respondents said they intend to vote against the initiative, while 34% plan on backing it.

Nearly all major political parties rejected the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP).

"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. "To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality."

Swiss foreign minister: Neutrality needs 'degree of flexibility'

Opponents of the initiative argued that in the modern world a country cannot hide behind neutrality and treat perpetrators and victims equally.

"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.

In-person voting will begin at 10:00 am (0800 GMT) and polling stations close at noon. The result should become clear around an hour later.

Another referendum on food security has also taken place with that initiative calling for the Swiss population to have access to enough high-quality and affordable food at all times.

According to SRF figures 28% of voters supported the initiative and 72% rejected it.

The food initiative seeks to have Switzerland produce significantly more of its own food.

entries.title: Germany news: Are Germans giving up their beloved meat and sausages?
entries.summary: Germans used to be all about sausages and meat. While those do remain popular, things seem to be slowly changing. There also are new insights into the economic side of East Germany's espionage DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: To eat or not to eat meat

Published September 26, 2026last updated September 27, 2026

Germans used to be all about sausages and meat. While those do remain popular, things seem to be slowly changing. There also are new insights into the economic side of East Germany's espionage DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germans grow more conscious about when to eat meat
  • Germany's Olympic committee decides Munich will bid to host the Games in 2036, 2040 or 2044
  • Former Chancellor Angela Merkel, a Protestant, wins top Catholic charity's prize

Follow our blog for the latest news and analysis from across Germany for the weekend of September 26-27, 2026.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section US politician suggests entry ban for German politicians seeking to ban far-right AfD

US politician suggests entry ban for German politicians seeking to ban far-right AfD

US Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna has reportedly threatened a travel ban to the US for German politicians who support banning the far-right AfD party. 

The AfD recently won massive vote shares in regional elections. Germany's intelligence service however has classified parts of the party as right-wing extremist. That's why many politicians and people in Germany think the party should in fact be banned. 

Anna Paulina Luna is a Republican and dedicated Trump supporter. According to German magazine Focus, she sent a letter to local MPs in Germany's state of Thuringia, in which she expresses support for the AfD, outrage at the proposed ban and raises the idea of refusing entry for German politicians who are publicly calling for a ban on the far-right party. 

Her letter comes as Thuringia's socialist Left Party has submitted a motion to start the process of banning the AfD. The Thuringia parliament will begin debating the motion next week. According to Focus, the AfD had asked the US politician to submit a statement on the matter.

Focus cites Luna's letter as saying that seeking to ban the AfD was a threat to democracy. She also said that, should the party indeed be banned, she'd talk to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about a travel ban for all those politicians who backed the plan.

While members of the AfD have welcomed Luna's involvement, politicians from the Left Party have sharply criticized it as an attempt to intimidate lawmakers.

Skip next section Two people killed as bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest

Two people killed as bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest

Two people were killed and more than 20 were injured when a bus carrying a group of tourists overturned on a motorway in southern Germany on Sunday.

Most passengers were reportedly from the Philippines and the bus was thought to have been headed for Munich's famous Oktoberfest. 

The accident happened in the early hours of the morning when the bus went off the side of a highway and overturned.

Munich's Oktoberfest draws millions of visitors from around the world every year, with large numbers of international tourists traveling to the Bavarian capital and surrounding region.

Skip next section Merz's conservatives no longer a big tent 'people's party'?

Merz's conservatives no longer a big tent 'people's party'?

Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the conservative party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, continues its soul-searching after its terrible results in recent regional elections.

While the party is generally considered to be more pro-business, it does have a workers' and employees’ wing and that part of the party is now warning the wider CDU that it is no longer a true Volkspartei, literally a "people’s party" or a big tent party.

Germany has two parties that traditionally have been considered a Volkspartei:  CDU on the center-right and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) on the center-left.

One of the two parties used to reliably get the biggest share of the vote, but that was not the case in elections in three German states this month.

The SPD has fallen further from its heyday, often coming only third or fourth in the polls. The poor showing of the CDU in recent elections in Saxony-Anhalt and especially Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania suggests the CDU is on a similar trajectory. Instead, it’s the far right and the far left that are gaining voters. 

In a new appeal, the CDU's employees' wing argues that too many people no longer feel represented by the party — and that the party risks becoming a political bubble talking mainly to itself.

The group says it wants the CDU to become more representative, not just in its rhetoric but in who actually gets involved and ends up in parliament. That means more people from different backgrounds and professions — from industry and skilled trades to healthcare, education and small businesses.

The group’s leadership also took aim at Chancellor Merz directly, saying that he had promised years ago to broaden the party’s appeal, but failed to do so.

Skip next section How Cold War espionage helped to boost East Germany's economy

How Cold War espionage helped to boost East Germany's economy

Would you think that espionage could significantly boost a country's economy? In the case of communist East Germany, that seems to have been the case — and to a significant degree. 

According to Reuters news agency, a study by the Rockwool Foundation suggests that espionage boosted East Germany's GDP by a whopping 7.4% in the 1970s and 80s.

How, you ask? Well, the notorious Stasi stole scientific and technical information from companies in the West, handed it to companies in the East and helped them increase productivity and growth.

"Stasi espionage strengthened East Germany's ​position within the socialist ‌bloc," said Albrecht Glitz, co-author of the study. "It did not, however, significantly improve success in ​Western markets."

The authors stressed that the East Germany case offers crucial insights for today, as countries again seek to protect strategic technologies, tighten export controls and screen foreign investment in sensitive industries.

 

Skip next section Berlin Marathon winner just shy of world record in dramatic finish

Berlin Marathon winner just shy of world record in dramatic finish

Even as the Berlin Marathon continues for many runners, the winners have already crossed the finish line.

In the Women's category, Ethiopia’s Tigst Assefa looked almost certain to set a new world record only to fall short in the very final stretch. It was only during the last kilometers that she appeared to struggle with a muscle injury or cramp.

She did win, clocking a time of 2:11:04, but did not beat Ruth Chepng'etich's world record of 2:09:56 from 2024.

Among the men racing in Berlin, fellow Ethiopian Guye Adola won the race, crossing the finish line at the Brandenburg Gate with a time of 2:02:51.

Skip next section Germans grow more conscious about (not) eating meat

Germans grow more conscious about (not) eating meat

Germany is famous for its variety of sausages and meats. But things seem to be changing somewhat and more people are eating less of some forms of meat — even if they're far from giving it up entirely.

A study in connection with World Vegetarian Day (on October 1) found 93% of households purchase meat. And the overall amount of meat bought hasn't actually gone down. That's only the case for sausages: Fewer people buy them and their overall sales have dropped.

According to the authors of the study, the data suggest that people are not necessarily moving toward vegetarianism or veganism. Instead, many are becoming more conscious about their diet and are trying to reduce their meat consumption without giving it up completely.

Around 43% of meat-eaters do concede that it would be better for them to eat less meat, and 27% say they do hope to buy less in the future. The favorite meat is chicken, followed by pork.

Meat substitutes are also becoming more popular with around 35% of households buying them.

Skip next section Welcome back

Welcome back

It's Sunday morning, and we're back with our coverage to keep you up to date on what's going on across Germany.

We'll see what the day will bring, but so far there'll be the question of whether Germans are eating less of their beloved (formerly beloved?) meat and sausages, there are new insights into the extent the notorious East German espionage helped to prop up the communist country's economy. We'll look at more soul-searching within Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union over how to react to the battering they received in recent regional elections.

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

We will be back on Sunday morning to bring you more of what's happening in Germany this weekend.

See you then!

Skip next section Germany Olympic bid: Munich named candidate city

Germany Olympic bid: Munich named candidate city

The German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) announced on Saturday that Munich has been chosen as Germany's candidate city to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics in either 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The Bavarian capital beat a rival Cologne-led bid from the western Rhine-Ruhr region.

Berlin had withdrawn its bid earlier in the week, while the residents of Hamburg voted against a bid in a referendum earlier this year.

Skip next section Mass protests against cuts to social services

Mass protests against cuts to social services

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets of cities across Germany on Saturday to voice their opposition to planned government spending cuts and call for a stronger welfare state.

Trade unions said a total of 175,000 took part in the protests, including in Nuremberg (over 20,000), Stuttgart (16,000), Frankfurt (15,000), Hanover (13,000), Essen (12,000), Berlin (5,500) and elsewhere under the slogan: "Hard-earned! Your work. Your health. Your pension."

Speaking in the western city of Essen, German Trade Union Confederation (DGB) leader Yasmin Fahimi criticized plans by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition government to reform working hours and pensions, and warned against cuts to social security benefits.

"We will not simply allow what we have built up over many years in terms of social standards to be taken away from us," she said.

Pension reform has been the focus of attention for months in Germany, while automobile giant Volkswagen has also announced sweeping job cuts.

The issues played a central role in the recent state elections in Berlin and the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which resulted in disastrous defeats for Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Nevertheless, the chancellor insisted earlier this month: "The reforms must go ahead."

Christiane Benner, leader of the trade union IG Metall, warned in Nuremberg against scaling back social security in times of restructuring and job cuts, for example in the automotive sector.

"Economic change can only succeed with confidence in the future and with solidarity," she said.

German employers, however, accused the trade unions of a "ritual refusal to reform."

Steffen Kampeter, chief executive of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), told the DPA news agency that "the trade unions say 'no' to almost every change" and accused them of "dreaming of the world of yesterday."

Skip next section Migration: Dobrindt calls for expanded Frontex role

Migration: Dobrindt calls for expanded Frontex role

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has called for an "expanded mandate" for the European Union's border protection agency Frontex when it comes to the deportation of illegal migrants.

"We are of the belief that we can strengthen the use of Frontex in deportation cases," he said ahead of a meeting of EU interior ministers in Munich on Saturday, calling for Frontex's area of operation to be expanded to "transit countries" outside the bloc.

"Of course, only with the agreement of these countries," he added.

Dobrindt said he also wanted to expand Frontex's responsibilities to "Dublin Regulations" – referring to the rules which determine which EU member state is responsible for the processing of an asylum application.

"A new European migration mechanism is needed," he said.

Skip next section Police close 2 autobahns to free giant wind-turbine

Police close 2 autobahns to free giant wind-turbine

A wide-load truck carrying a nearly 100-meter-long (328-feet-long) wind turbine blade forced the closure of two motorways in western Germany after it got stuck along a narrow section of the carriageway.

The daily Bild newspaper reported that the truck was traveling along the A43 autobahn near the Recklinghausen interchange in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia when the dramatic incident unfolded on Wednesday evening.

Police said the driver ignored warning signs that the highway was unsuitable for heavy-load vehicles.

"The highway is not permitted for heavy transport vehicles in that area. They have to exit because the route crosses the Rhine-Herne Canal a little further on," a spokesperson for Münster Police's highway patrol told Bild.

An automatic barrier and weighing system is meant to prevent loads over 3.5 tons from crossing an old bridge over the canal.

After initially blocking traffic on A43, the truck was ordered onto the hard shoulder to allow traffic to restart along one remaining open lane.

The police spokesperson said "several attempts" were made to free the truck with its ultra-wide cargo over the next two days.

On Friday night, the driver agreed to reverse his truck onto the nearby A2, which forced the temporary closure of a second autobahn, before being allowed to continue his journey just after midnight on Saturday.

Skip next section Rail services canceled, delayed after suspected cable theft

Rail services canceled, delayed after suspected cable theft

Police blamed disruption to high-speed rail services in western Germany on deliberate damage to signal cabling overnight.

National rail operator Deutsche Bahn said trains running between Dortmund and Munich, Hamburg and Basel, and northern Germany and Cologne faced cancellations, delays and diversions.

According to the Zuginfo.nrw website, the entire Gelsenkirchen metropolitan area is currently impassable.

A police spokesman said officers were investigating suspected cable theft on a railway line in Gelsenkirchen-Ückendorf, where signals and control systems had failed.

The suspects are believed to have crudely cut and ripped out cables beside the tracks at several points.

It is unclear how long the repair work will take.

Skip next section Caritas honors Merkel with prize for social cohesion

Caritas honors Merkel with prize for social cohesion

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel, a Protestant, received one of the highest honors of the Catholic Church's social welfare charity in Germany.

The 72-year-old was awarded the Elisabeth Prize by the Catholic Caritas Association at an event in the southern city of Augsburg on Friday evening.

The prize is named after Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia, who lived from 1207 to 1231 and who helped people in need. She is the patron saint of Caritas.

The honor recognized Merkel's commitment to social cohesion, with Caritas President Eva Welskop-Deffaa paying tribute to the "inner compass with which she [Merkel] successfully steered the country's fortunes."

The former chancellor told the roughly 400 guests that "there will always be a need for people to be there for one another."

Once seen by some as Mutti — Germany’s reassuring mother figure — Merkel has become an increasingly divisive figure because of her 2015 decision to open the borders to more than a million refugees.

Critics say Merkel’s decision fueled years of backlash that helped turn the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from a fringe protest party into a force that now leads most national polls.

Skip next section Dobrindt seeks 'hardening' of EU borders at Munich talks

Dobrindt seeks 'hardening' of EU borders at Munich talks

Several European Union interior ministers are meeting in Munich this afternoon to discuss tightening the bloc's migration policy.

A spokesperson for German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Münchner Merkur newspaper that the talks will focus on the "implementation of a shift in migration policy."

The 17 ministers will discuss "further refining the European Migration Pact, consistently hardening the European Union's external borders, and accelerating returns from Europe," the spokesperson added.

Germany and Denmark, Austria, the Netherlands, and Greece are due to hold separate talks about the creation of deportation centers or return hubs in third countries.

Germany hopes to secure a deal with a country in Africa or possibly Asia by the end of the year.

Dobrindt's spokesperson said the EU's border agency, Frontex, could be turned into a "border protection and genuine return agency."

Currently, EU member states are responsible for returning asylum seekers whose applications have failed.

EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner will also attend the Munich talks.

entries.title: Northern Ireland: Pro-UK march to go through Catholic area
entries.summary: It's the first time the march has been allowed to go through the area since 1997. Overnight, a court ruling allowed it to take place after a series of last-minute legal challenges that reached Belfast's High Court.
entries.content:
Ireland

Northern Ireland: Pro-UK march to go through Catholic area

September 27, 2026

It's the first time the march has been allowed to go through the area since 1997. Overnight, a court ruling allowed it to take place after a series of last-minute legal challenges that reached Belfast's High Court.

Northern Ireland's Protestant, pro-British Orange Order was set to parade through a mainly Catholic and nationalist area on Sunday.

It's the first time the march has been allowed to go through the area since 1997. Overnight, a court ruling allowed it to take place after a series of last-minute legal challenges that reached Belfast's High Court.

Thirty-five members of the Orange Order are to march silently through Garvaghy Road in the town of Portadown, without any bands or other Order supporters participating.

About 2,000 people gathered on the street Sunday morning in a counterprotest to prevent the march.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for "calm on all sides." In a BBC interview, he said "big gains" had been made in Northern Ireland "and we don't want to see things go backwards."

Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, a member of the Irish republican Sinn Fein party, spoke against the decision to allow the march to take place.

"Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever," she said, also voicing her support for the local residents to protest against the march, which she labeled "unwanted" and "sectarian."

Carla Lockhart, an MP from the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said local residents have nothing to fear from "thirty five men walking down a road silently and with no bands and in an orderly fashion."

History of conflict

Garvaghy Road was one of the epicenters of the conflict between the Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and the Protestant, pro-British unionists in the late 1990s.

Back then, clashes between residents and the marchers repeatedly triggered disorder, also known as the Drumcree dispute.

As part of the Good Friday Agreement, a deal signed in 1998 that largely ended three decades of conflict between the two sides known as the Troubles, an entity was established to regulate contentious processions named The Parades Commission.

The Commission repeatedly rejected the Orange Order's requests to march through the area, with a High Court ruling quashing the rejection this year due to a procedural error. The Order then issued a fresh application, which was approved.

entries.title: India news: Kolkata's SRFTI students allege violent attack
entries.summary: Students at Kolkata's Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute say they were attacked with knives after confronting an outside group over a meeting they allege was affiliated with the right-wing Hindu RSS.
entries.content:
India

India news: SRFTI students violently attacked in Kolkata

Published September 26, 2026last updated September 27, 2026

Students at Kolkata's Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute say they were attacked with knives after confronting an outside group over a meeting they allege was affiliated with the right-wing Hindu RSS.

Skip next section SRFTI students attacked after objecting to outsiders' event on campus

SRFTI students attacked after objecting to outsiders' event on campus

Students of the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) in Kolkata said on Sunday they were violently attacked after objecting to a meeting held on campus by an allegedly rightwing group, a student representative told DW.

A scuffle broke out between the students and members of the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat (ABGP) after the student union confronted the group saying it had not been informed about the meeting and questioned the participants before the confrontation turned violent.

The students allege that members of the group attacked them with knives.

Poorvi Bondre, an editing student from Maharashtra and a member of the SRFTI student union, told DW that the event was affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and was being used to promote its agenda on campus.

She said students had opposed the meeting because it was not a film screening but what she described as direct RSS promotion.

The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization and the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"This was an RSS event. We were completely unaware of this event. When we asked them what this was about, the fight started," Bondre said. "They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives."

Videos of the incident have circulated on social media, showing students with what appear to be knife wounds. However, DW could not independently verify their authenticity.

The campus remains tense, with students inside and members of the ABGP gathered outside, according to the student representative.

Skip next section Modi says India follows 'zero tolerance' policy against terrorism

Modi says India follows 'zero tolerance' policy against terrorism

Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Sunday that India follows a "zero tolerance" policy against terrorism, ahead of the 10th anniversary of the 2016 strikes against targets in Pakistan.

Speaking on his "Mann Ki Baat" radio program, Modi linked the 2016 strikes, carried out after an attack that killed 19 Indian soldiers, with the 2019 Balakot airstrikes and 2025's Operation Sindoor, saying India had repeatedly sent the same message to Pakistan over the past decade.

Meanwhile, Defense Minister Rajnath Singh separately said India was prepared to carry out any strike against terrorism if anu neighboring country continued what he described as a "state policy of terrorism," the Hindustan Times reported.

Singh said India sought peace and dialogue but would not compromise on national security, according to the report.

"India wants peace, but India will not compromise on its security under any circumstances," Singh was quoted as saying by the newspaper. "India believes in dialogue. India believes in dialogue, but if any country gives shelter to terrorism against India, then the scope of dialogue ends right there."

Skip next section Jaishankar meets Canadian foreign minister, says ties ready for 'higher level'

Jaishankar meets Canadian foreign minister, says ties ready for 'higher level'

Indian External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met with Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly as the two countries attempt to rebuild frayed ties,  

Jaishankar referred to the meeting as a "productive discussion" as New Delhi and Ottawa "prepare to take the relationship to a higher level."

Ties between the two countries were tested following the killing of Sikh separatist leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar in 2023, which triggered a major diplomatic dispute between India and Canada.

Skip next section More than 56 killed, 1,000 houses destroyed as heavy rains lash Uttar Pradesh

More than 56 killed, 1,000 houses destroyed as heavy rains lash Uttar Pradesh

At least 56 people died due to heavy rain and storms in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh over the past three days, authorities said on Sunday.

The deaths were reported across India's most populous state, where 63 districts were affected.

According to a statement by the state disaster management department, "exceptionally heavy rain that has affected much of Uttar Pradesh."

More than 1,000 houses were damaged, while several people were also left injured, authorities said.

The Relief Commissioner's office's statement said the state recorded 66.5 millimeters (2.62 inches) of rain between Friday and Sunday, compared to the season average of 7.6 millimeters.

Last month, heavy rainfall and thunderstorms claimed dozens of lives across India, as the country grapples with extreme weather.

Skip next section Cricket: Kohli says 2027 ODI World Cup will be his last

Cricket: Kohli says 2027 ODI World Cup will be his last

Indian cricketer and one of the game's biggest global stars, Virat Kohli announced on Saturday that the 2027 ODI World Cup will be his last for India, as the veteran batter looks for another title.

"For ​me, it's ‌the last World Cup I'm going to play for India," Kohli told broadcaster JioStar on Saturday.

The 37-year-old, who now plays only One Day International (ODI) cricket, said he was motivated to "leave everything out there" and help India win the tournament.

"‌And, of course, the goal is absolutely to win the World Cup ‌and ​whatever it takes, I'm absolutely ready."

Kohli has scored 14,941 ODI runs and a record 54 centuries, and was part of India's 2011 World Cup-winning team. He retired from T20 internationals after India's 2024 World Cup victory and from Test cricket last year.

The 2027 ODI Cricket World Cup will be held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Skip next section At least 19 dead in Nagaland due to spurious liquor

At least 19 dead in Nagaland due to spurious liquor

At least 19 people have died in the northeastern state of Nagaland after allegedly consuming suspected spurious liquor, prompting a police probe and crackdown on illegal alcohol, local media reports said on Sunday.

Eight deaths were reported in Mokokchung district and 11 in Tuensang, while police have arrested 19 people and seized nearly 3,000 bottles of liquor.

A Special Investigation Team has been formed to trace the source and supply chain, with liquor samples sent for forensic examination, authorities said.

Skip next section CJP leader Ashutosh Ranka detained by Assam Police, Dipke says

CJP leader Ashutosh Ranka detained by Assam Police, Dipke says

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, posted on X on Sunday that CJP co-convener Ashutosh Ranka has been detained by the police in the northeastern state of Assam while on a visit to the state.

Earlier, Ranka talked to reporters in Assam, where he targeted the chief minister.

"Himanta Biswa Sarma is scared that if we expose the reality of Assam's schools, the country will find out what the condition of the schools here is really like," Ranka said.

The CJP leader said the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader is "scared that people will find out how the rights of the people are being taken away in Kaziranga, and how their water, forests and land are being taken away and handed over to their corporate allies."

He accused Sarma of being scared that "people will find out how manmade floods were created in Assam, and how hundreds of people lost their lives."

Ranka also brought up the delimitation in Assam in 2023, which critics say altered demographic weights.

"We know how you redraw the boundaries of the constituencies during the assembly elections," Ranka said. "In one village, people ended up voting in three different constituencies, simply so that you could rig the election and win. But we are not people who are going to be afraid."

Skip next section Protests, vandalism at Punjab's university over rape allegations

Protests, vandalism at Punjab's university over rape allegations

Large student protests erupted overnight on Saturday at Lovely Professional University in Punjab's Phagwara, after claims circulated on social media that a female student had allegedly been raped and subsequently died by suicide, according to reports.

Videos showed students smashing windows and flower pots, while some objects and parts of the private university building were set on fire.

However, some students posted on social media that the vandals were not university students but outsiders.

Reports also said students blocked the Jalandhar–Phagwara National Highway. Ppolice later cleared the highway.

Kapurthala Superintendent of Police Gaurav Toora said police had received no complaint or information about any rape and learned of the allegations only after reaching the campus.

Police said a report has been registered based on a students' statement, while investigators are examining the allegation and CCTV footage.

The university urged students to ignore the "rumors" and said they were safe, media reports said.

Skip next section ECI frames new rules for voter roll revisions amid furor

ECI frames new rules for voter roll revisions amid furor

India's Election Commission (ECI) on Saturday said all decisions concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously, amid reports of differences within the poll panel, media reports said.

At a meeting, chaired by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, held on Saturday, the commission also eased the process for voters who receive notices over discrepancies, the reports said.

According to the reports, the new mandates for those who receive notices:

  • local electoral officials will visit homes to collect documents and upload them into the Election Commission's system
  • hearings only in exceptional cases, preferably online
  • an authorized adult family member can appear on behalf of a voter
  • help desks and special enrollment drives for people who were left off electoral rolls, including first-time voters
  • an independent expert would review the ECI's system for compliance with electoral laws

The ECI, while extending the deadline for claims and objections in Delhi to October 30 and in Maharashtra to October 12, said SIR had been completed in 20 states and Union territories, including Bihar and West Bengal, the reports said.

As deadly heat threatens livelihoods, women working in Delhi's informal sector are trying out heat wave insurance that pays out automatically when temperatures spike.

Skip next section India opposition INDIA bloc to meet over voter roll revision

India opposition INDIA bloc to meet over voter roll revision

The opposition INDIA bloc parties are likely to meet in New Delhi on September 30 to discuss concerns over the Election Commission of India (ECI) and its Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rollsand a coordinated joint response, the Times of India newspaper reported on Saturday.

The proposed meeting comes amid growing calls for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after an Indian Express investigation found that Kumar's fellow Election Commissioners had raised at least 14 objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registration and electoral data.

The three commissioners are overseeing the SIR, a voter-roll revision that the ECI says aims to remove the names of deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Critics, however, say the exercise has gone beyond that remit and resulted in the removal of millions of eligible voters, potentially benefiting the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

On Friday, Congress workers staged protests across several states demanding Kumar's resignation. Police used water cannons and detained protesters in several locations as they attempted to march towards election offices.

Congress has called for an independent audit of the revision process and greater transparency over deleted and restored voters.

entries.title: Iran sticks to Hormuz plan after Trump rejects it
entries.summary: Iranian officials that while they were aware of Trump's comments on rejecting the new proposal, they had not received a formal message rejecting the plan that would open the Strait of Hormuz.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran sticks to Hormuz plan after Trump rejects it

September 27, 2026

Iranian officials that while they were aware of Trump's comments on rejecting the new proposal, they had not received a formal message rejecting the plan that would open the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran on Sunday insisted on its conditions for reopeningthe Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump's public rejection of the proposal that had birthed some hope for reopening the key waterway.

"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday, according to state broadcaster IRIB.

"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights," he said.

Iran proposed a seven-day plan aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within days.

Tehran said it had transmitted the proposal to Washington via Qatari mediators.

Iran's plan, Araghchi said, called for cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including Lebanon, and fulfilling the conditions of the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago. That agreement called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

Trump rejects plan, but no communication to Iran

Trump publicly rejected Iran's proposal on Saturday while speaking to reporters at the White House.

"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," he said. "They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly."

Responding to Trump's comments, Araghchi said Iranians "saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators."

"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them," the foreign minister added.

The strait stalemate

Iranian ports are currently under a US blockade as Washington attempts to pressure Tehran into lifting its closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The key waterway remains largely shut to international shipping despite Trump's claims that the US controls it.

Early Sunday, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) — set up by Iran to manage the Strait of Hormuz — warned ships of consequences if they use "illegal routes" in the region.

"This risks financial and life losses for the vessel, owner, master and crew, and seriously restricts its future Strait of Hormuz passage," it said in a post on X.

The authority said if ships breach its rules, all vessels belonging to the company could face restrictions in the future.

Around a fifth of global oil demand passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war began. The waterway is also a crucial route for liquefied natural gas and fertilizer.

entries.title: No public mentions of Taiwan at official Xi and Trump meeting
entries.summary: At a high-profile summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington, there was much talk of trade and artificial intelligence. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was only discussed in private.
entries.content:
United States of America

Taiwan not openly discussed at Xi and Trump meeting

September 27, 2026

At a high-profile summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington, there was much talk of trade and artificial intelligence. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was only discussed in private.

US President Donald Trump picked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping up directly from the airport and in his welcoming remarks he praised the strong friendship between their two nations, as well as recalling how China and the US fought together as allies during World War II.

"Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II," he said. "Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country," he said at the White House, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that fought alongside China against the Japanese between 1941 and 1942.

However, these pilots did not actually volunteer to fight with the People's Republic of China, whose leader was visiting Washington and which was not founded until 1949. The Americans were risking their lives for the former Republic of China, whose government relocated to Taiwan after  communist victory in the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

"China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen," Trump said at a state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening. Sun Yat-sen was the founder of the Republic of China in 1912 and the Kuomintang, or KMT, which remains a major political party in Taiwan today.

Taiwan a major problem between US and China

Ever since the end of World War II, Taiwan has been a point of contention between Beijing and Washington. For decades, the US government ignored the communist regime in the People's Republic of China. But since 1972, Washington has acknowledged the "one China principle," according to which there is only one China, whose legal government is in Beijing and Taiwan belongs to it. Diplomatic relations between the US and China were only established in 1979.

The Taiwan Relations Act came into effect in 1979 too. The US law legalized arms exports to Taiwan. It also allowed the US government to take military action to prevent changes to the status quo in the Taiwan Strait.

A potential war between China and Taiwan would not only jeopardize stability in the Asia-Pacific region but also plunge the global economy into a prolonged recession, as supply chains would be severely disrupted.

During their high-profile meeting, Xi did not openly urge the US to respect the "one China" principle as he has done in the past, and Trump did not mention Taiwan in public either. In May, he put on hold a $14-billion arms deal that the US had concluded with the Taiwanese government late last year. The arms sales deal remains under review.

"Given the US' production capacity and its own military needs, it will take some time before approved arms can be delivered," said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist and professor at the National University of Singapore. "It remains unclear what else the US can currently offer Taiwan."

Ahead of crucial midterm elections in November, Trump urgently needs some positive headlines. He and his Republican party rely on farmers for support so they need China to import US agricultural goods. In 2023, before their current trade war, China imported $43 billion worth of soy, beef, wood and other goods from the US. However Beijing has drastically reduced its imports since.

Taiwan mentioned behind closed doors

China used the meeting "to make clear to Trump its opposition to any US military support for Taiwan," said William Yang, an analyst with the International Crisis Group. "Xi wants to convey this message personally and behind closed doors, thereby influencing Trump's decision on arms sales to Taiwan."

China's Xinhua news agency said that Xi had addressed the issue behind closed doors. It reported that Xi had expressed hope that the US would take strong action against Taiwanese independence and said that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was clear. He reportedly added that "building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability is neither an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight."

It will not have pleased Taiwanese politicians that the US president openly considered treating Taiwan as a bargaining chip in its negotiations with China, German sinologist Eberhard Sandschneider of the consultancy Berlin Global Advisers suggested during a political chatshow on German public television. "People living on the island of Taiwan do not take this lightly. This is an existential issue for Taiwan."

He added that he did not think China would take military action against Taiwan. That would be a move just as illogical as the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US attack on Iran, he argued.

Nobody is playing poker in China, Sandschneider continued. "Clear strategic interests are pursued there. National sovereignty and winning back Taiwan are key concerns. At the same time, it is well known that any military attack on Taiwan would not only lead to a military disaster but also to an economic collapse. The resulting setback for the global economy would call into question the Communist Party's legitimacy," the expert said.

De Zheng contributed to this article, which has been translated from German.
